# Before you write code {background-color="#1a81c2"}

## What is Bioconductor?

- A repository of **open-source R packages** for analysing and understanding
  **high-throughput biological data**
- \> 2,300 software packages, plus annotation and experiment data packages
- Two releases per year (~April and ~October), each tied to an R version
- A **community**: developers, reviewers, support site, Zulip chat, conferences

<br>

. . .

Packages are **reviewed before acceptance** and **built and checked
nightly** on Linux, macOS and Windows.

## Is my package in scope?

Bioconductor packages should address the analysis of **high-throughput
biological data**: sequencing, microarrays, flow cytometry, mass
spectrometry, imaging, single-cell, etc.

. . .

<br>

Core principles:

- **Interoperability**: reuse Bioconductor data structures and infrastructure
- **Best practices**: complete documentation, executed vignettes, unit tests
- **Commitment** to maintaining the package and answering user questions

## Scope is described with **biocViews**

*biocViews* are terms from a controlled vocabulary that classify packages.
They're shown on the landing page and are used for searching.

```{r}
#| label: biocviews
#| comment: ""
#| code-fold: true
views <- read.dcf(
    url("https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/VIEWS"),
    fields = c("Package", "biocViews")
)
pkgs <- c("DESeq2", "scater")
v <- views[views[, "Package"] %in% pkgs, ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(v))) {
    cat(v[i, "Package"], ":\n", sep = "")
    cat(strwrap(gsub("\n", " ", v[i, "biocViews"]), indent = 4, exdent = 4,
                width = 75), sep = "\n")
}
```

## Choosing biocViews

- Browse the hierarchy at
  [bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html)
- Pick **at least two leaf terms** (the most specific ones) from the same
  trunk
- Terms are **case-sensitive**, and must be on a single comma-separated line

```default
biocViews: Software, Transcriptomics, RNASeq, Normalization, GeneExpression
```

. . .

<br>

::: {.keybox}
💡 Look at the biocViews of packages similar to yours. You'll often find
terms you hadn't thought of.
:::

## Types of Bioconductor packages

| Type | What it contains | Example |
|------|------------------|---------|
| **Software** | Algorithms, data access, visualisation (most packages) | `DESeq2`, `scater` |
| **Annotation** | Database-like packages that map IDs to other information | `org.Hs.eg.db` |
| **Experiment data** | Data sets to illustrate analyses and methods | `airway` |
| **Workflow** | Long-form vignettes showing multi-package analyses | `rnaseqGene` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,55,25]"}

<br>

::: {.muted}
For large data, consider
[AnnotationHub](https://bioconductor.org/packages/AnnotationHub) and
[ExperimentHub](https://bioconductor.org/packages/ExperimentHub) instead of
packaging the data. There are also
[Bioconductor books](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/).
:::

## What makes a good package?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Integration with the ecosystem**

- **Interoperability**: take and return Bioconductor classes
- **Don't reinvent the wheel**: reuse existing import functions,
  classes and methods
- **Lightweight**: as few dependencies as possible
- **Tested and documented**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Small, focused functions**

- Each function does **one thing** (split anything longer than a screen)
- A **consistent API**: similar argument names across functions, `camelCase` or `snake_case`.
- Few exported functions that users actually need; helpers stay internal
  (`.helperName()`)
:::

::::

## Tools that make development easier

| Package | Functionality |
|---------|-------------------|
| [usethis](https://usethis.r-lib.org/) | Creating packages and files: `create_package()`, `use_r()`, `use_test()`, `use_vignette()` |
| [devtools](https://devtools.r-lib.org/) | Development cycle: `load_all()`, `document()`, `test()`, `check()` |
| [roxygen2](https://roxygen2.r-lib.org/) | Writing documentation and `NAMESPACE` from comments in R code |
| [testthat](https://testthat.r-lib.org/) + [covr](https://covr.r-lib.org/) | Unit tests and test coverage |
| [biocthis](https://bioconductor.org/packages/biocthis) | Bioconductor-flavoured templates: `use_bioc_description()`, `use_bioc_vignette()`, `use_bioc_github_action()` |
| [BiocCheck](https://bioconductor.org/packages/BiocCheck) | Bioconductor-specific checks before submission |

: {.smaller tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

## A typical development workflow

```r
# Step 1: Create the skeleton of a new package
usethis::create_package("~/Documents/toyBioc")

# Step 2: Add Bioconductor-style files with biocthis
biocthis::use_bioc_description()        # DESCRIPTION with biocViews etc.
biocthis::use_bioc_vignette("toyBioc")  # vignette template with BiocStyle
biocthis::use_bioc_github_action()      # GitHub Actions to check the package

## Step 3: Write code and tests
usethis::use_r("normalizeCounts")       # creates R/normalizeCounts.R
usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts")    # creates tests/testthat/test-normalizeCounts.R

## The development loop: repeat until happy
devtools::load_all()                    # load the package (like library())
devtools::document()                    # update man/ and NAMESPACE
devtools::test()                        # run unit tests
devtools::check()                       # run R CMD check
```

## DESCRIPTION

```default
Package: toyBioc
Title: Normalization of RNA-seq Count Matrices
Version: 0.99.0
Authors@R:
    person("Fabrício", "Almeida-Silva", email = "fabricio@example.com",
           role = c("aut", "cre"), comment = c(ORCID = "0000-0000-0000-0000"))
Description: toyBioc provides functions to normalize RNA-seq count data
    stored in matrices and SummarizedExperiment objects. It implements
    counts per million (CPM) and log-transformed CPM. It also provides
    diagnostic plots to compare samples before and after normalization.
License: GPL-3
URL: https://github.com/username/toyBioc
BugReports: https://github.com/username/toyBioc/issues
biocViews: Software, Transcriptomics, RNASeq, Normalization
Imports: SummarizedExperiment, methods, stats
Suggests: BiocStyle, knitr, rmarkdown, testthat (>= 3.0.0), ggplot2
VignetteBuilder: knitr
```

New packages start at version **0.99.0**. There's exactly **one
maintainer** (`cre`), with an email address you actively read.

## DESCRIPTION: advertise your package

The `Description` field is shown at the top of your package's **landing
page**. It's often the first thing potential users read.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
```default
Description: Normalize data.
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
```default
Description: toyBioc provides functions to
    normalize RNA-seq count data stored in
    matrices and SummarizedExperiment
    objects. It implements counts per million
    (CPM) and log-transformed CPM, and
    provides diagnostic plots to compare
    samples before and after normalization.
```
:::
:::

::::

- At least **3 complete sentences**: what does it do, for which data, and
  why should I use it?
- A **brief but descriptive** `Title`

## DESCRIPTION: Depends, Imports, Suggests

| Field | Used for | |
|-------|-----------|-|
| `Imports` | Packages whose functions or classes your code uses | Most packages go here |
| `Suggests` | Packages used only in vignettes, examples, tests, or optional code | `knitr`, `testthat`, `BiocStyle` |
| `Depends` | Packages users *always* need attached with yours (e.g., infrastructure pkgs) | Rarely needed; more than 3 is unusual |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,50,32]"}

<br>

- Each package should appear in **only one** of these fields
- **Bioconductor packages in `Imports`**: interoperability

## Mind the number of dependencies

Dependencies can break and/or make package installation slower.

```{r}
#| label: deps
deps <- tools::package_dependencies(
    c("S4Vectors", "SummarizedExperiment"),
    db = installed.packages(), recursive = TRUE
)
lengths(deps)
```

. . .

Before adding a dependency, ask yourself:

- Do I need the whole package for **one small function**?
- Is the function used in the **core** of my package, or in a niche feature?

## Move niche dependencies to Suggests

A heavy package used only in one rarely-used function can go to `Suggests`.

```r
plotDensities <- function(se) {
    if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
        stop("Package 'ggplot2' is required for this function. ",
             "Install it with BiocManager::install('ggplot2').")
    }
    df <- .longFormat(se)
    ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x = value, colour = sample)) +
        ggplot2::geom_density()
}
```

<br>

::: {.keybox}
💡 Use `pkg::fun()` for packages in `Suggests`. Don't import them in
`NAMESPACE`.
:::

## DESCRIPTION: License

- Bioconductor packages must be **open-source**: use a standard license and
  give its version
  - `GPL-3`, `GPL-2`, `Artistic-2.0` (common in core packages), `MIT + file LICENSE`, ...
- Licenses that **restrict use** are **not suitable**:
  - `CC BY-NC 4.0`, `CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`, `CC BY-NC-ND 4.0` (no commercial
    use), `ACM`
- Check that your license is compatible with the licenses of your
  dependencies (and of any third-party code you include)

## NAMESPACE

List of **imports** and **exports** created automatically by 
{roxygen2} from `@export` and `@importFrom` tags.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
```r
#' @import SummarizedExperiment
#' @import ggplot2
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
```r
#' @importFrom SummarizedExperiment assay
#' @importFrom stats median
```
:::
:::

::::

Running `devtools::document()` creates the NAMESPACE file:

```default
# Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand
export(normalizeCounts)
importFrom(SummarizedExperiment,assay)
importFrom(stats,median)
```

## R/: what a function looks like

```{r}
#| label: show-function
#| echo: false
#| class-output: r
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines(file.path(toy_path, "R/normalizeCounts.R"))[17:30], sep = "\n")
```

- **Validate inputs** early (here, in the internal helper `.checkCounts()`)
- 4 spaces of indentation, ≤ 80 characters per line, `<-` for assignment

## R/: documenting functions with roxygen2

```r
#' Normalize a matrix of RNA-seq counts
#'
#' @param counts A numeric matrix of raw read counts, with genes in rows
#'     and samples in columns.
#' @param method Character indicating the normalization method. One of
#'     "cpm" (counts per million) or "log2cpm" (log2 of CPM + 1).
#'     Default: "cpm".
#'
#' @return A numeric matrix with the same dimensions as `counts`,
#'     containing normalized expression values.
#'
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' counts <- matrix(c(10, 0, 5, 20, 3, 7), nrow = 3)
#' normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm")
normalizeCounts <- function(counts, method = c("cpm", "log2cpm")) {
```

`devtools::document()` creates `man/normalizeCounts.Rd` and updates
`NAMESPACE`. **Every exported** function needs a man page with 
**runnable examples** 

## Docs: say what each parameter *is*

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
```r
#' @param counts Counts.
#' @param method Method to use.
#' @param min_count Minimum count.
#' @param plot Whether to plot or not.
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
```r
#' @param counts A numeric matrix of raw
#'     read counts, with genes in rows and
#'     samples in columns.
#' @param method Character indicating the
#'     normalization method. One of "cpm" or
#'     "log2cpm". Default: "cpm".
#' @param min_count Numeric scalar indicating
#'     the minimum count for a gene to be kept.
#'     Default: 10.
#' @param plot Logical indicating whether to
#'     plot densities. Default: FALSE.
```
:::
:::
::::

State the **class** (numeric, character, logical, `SummarizedExperiment`,
...), the **expected shape** (scalar, vector, matrix), the **valid values**,
and the **default**.

## Docs: describe what's returned

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.bad}
```r
#' @return A data frame with
#'     the results.
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.good}
```r
#' @return A data frame with the
#'     following columns:
#'     \describe{
#'       \item{gene}{Character, gene ID.}
#'       \item{logFC}{Numeric, log2 fold
#'         change (treatment vs control).}
#'       \item{pvalue}{Numeric, P-value.}
#'       \item{padj}{Numeric, P-value adjusted
#'         for multiple testing (BH method).}
#'       \item{significant}{Logical, whether
#'         `padj` < `alpha`.}
#'     }
```
:::
:::
::::

When a function returns a data frame (or a list), document **every column
(or element)** and its **type**.

## Code: some do's and don'ts

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
```r
# Bad 1: if `x` is empty
lapply(1:length(x), ...)

# Bad 2: type not explicit
res <- sapply(x, mean)

# Bad 3: 2+ classes, inheritance
if(class(se) == "SummarizedExperiment")

# Bad 4: `T` can be a variable
normalizeCounts(counts, log = T)

# Bad 5: `cat()` cannot be silenced
cat("Normalizing", n, "samples...\n")

# Bad 6: `set.seed()` inside code 
set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(ncol(counts), 10)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
```r
# Good 1: empty sequence with empty `x`
lapply(seq_along(x), ...)

# Good 2: explicit type
res <- vapply(x, mean, numeric(1))

# Good 3: inheritance handled
if(is(se, "SummarizedExperiment"))

# Good 4: `TRUE` or `FALSE
normalizeCounts(counts, log = TRUE)

# Good 5: `message()`/`warning()`/`stop()`
message("Normalizing ", n, " samples...")

# Good 6: let users set the seed
idx <- sample(ncol(counts), 10)
```
:::
:::

::::

See the full list [here](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/r-code.html#r-code-best-practices-and-guidelines).

## R/: S4 classes, a short example

Before creating a new class, check whether an existing one can hold your
data (or be **extended**). If you do need one:

```{r}
#| label: s4-class
setClass("CountSet",
    slots = c(counts = "matrix", condition = "factor"),
    validity = function(object) {
        if (ncol(object@counts) != length(object@condition))
            return("ncol(counts) must equal length(condition)")
        TRUE
    }
)

## A constructor (users never call new() directly)
CountSet <- function(counts, condition) {
    new("CountSet", counts = counts, condition = factor(condition))
}
```

## R/: S4 generics, methods and show()

```{r}
#| label: s4-methods
setGeneric("counts", function(object) standardGeneric("counts"))
setMethod("counts", "CountSet", function(object) object@counts)

setMethod("show", "CountSet", function(object) {
    cat("CountSet with", nrow(object@counts), "genes and",
        ncol(object@counts), "samples\n")
    cat("Conditions:", levels(object@condition), "\n")
})

cs <- CountSet(matrix(rpois(20, 10), nrow = 5), rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), 2))
cs
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: s4-validity
#| error: true
CountSet(matrix(rpois(20, 10), nrow = 5), c("ctrl", "trt"))
```

## tests/: write tests right after the code

Tests check if your functions work as expected, and should be written early.

```r
usethis::use_r("normalizeCounts")     # 1. write the function in R/
usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts")  # 2. write its tests, right away
devtools::load_all()                  # 3. load the package...
devtools::test()                      #    ...run the tests, and repeat
```

. . .

Advantages of writing tests early:

- You still remember the **edge cases** you had in mind while writing the code
- Bugs are caught **early**, when they're easy to fix
- You can **refactor** later with confidence: tests tell you if you broke
  something
- Tests **document** how the function is supposed to behave


## tests/: writing unit tests with {testthat}

```r
usethis::use_testthat()               # tests/testthat.R + tests/testthat/
usethis::use_test("normalizeCounts")  # tests/testthat/test-normalizeCounts.R
```

```{r}
#| label: show-tests
#| echo: false
#| class-output: r
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines(file.path(toy_path, "tests/testthat/test-normalizeCounts.R")),
    sep = "\n")
```

## tests/: how much of my code is tested?

```{r}
#| label: covr
#| output: asis
cov <- covr::package_coverage(toy_path)
cat(render_coverage_html(cov, toy_path, from_line = 17))
```

::: {.fragment}
`r sprintf("Coverage: %.1f%%", covr::percent_coverage(cov))`. The lines in
red have **never been executed** by the tests: the `"log2cpm"` option and the
warning for `NA`s.
:::

## tests/: covering all lines

Add tests for **every option** of each argument and **every error or
warning** your code can raise:

```r
test_that("normalizeCounts() returns log2-CPM values", {
    lcpm <- normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm")
    expect_equal(lcpm, log2(normalizeCounts(counts) + 1))
})

test_that("normalizeCounts() warns about NAs", {
    counts_na <- counts
    counts_na[1, 1] <- NA
    expect_warning(normalizeCounts(counts_na), "NA values")
})
```

- Test **edge cases**: `NA`s, empty inputs, a single sample, all zeros
- Simulate failures, e.g., a file that doesn't exist or invalid input
- Look at coverage interactively with `covr::report()`

## tests/: good testing practices

**Use toy data sets**

- Small objects created in the test file or in `tests/testthat/helper-*.R`
- Or small example data that ships with the package (`data/`, `inst/extdata/`)
- Tests should run in **seconds**

. . .

**Avoid over-testing**

- Test **behaviour** (inputs → outputs), not implementation details
- Don't test other packages' functions
- Avoid many near-duplicate tests
- 100% coverage is not a goal in itself

## Package structure: src/ {.anatomy-slide}

```{r}
#| label: anatomy-src
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(render_anatomy(c("src")))
```

## src/: do you really need it?

`src/` is **optional**. Most Bioconductor packages are written in pure R.

Cost of compiled code:

- Users (and Bioconductor's build machines) need **compilers** and system
  libraries on Linux, macOS and Windows
- Builds can fail on one platform only, and memory errors (segfaults) are
  **hard to debug**
- Fewer people can **review**, contribute to, and maintain the code

## src/: do you really need it? (cont'd)

Only add compiled code in the (rare) cases where **well-written R code is
still too slow**, and you have **measured** that it is. The workflow:

1. Write correct R code, with tests
2. **Profile** it to find the bottleneck
3. Optimise the bottleneck in R, and **benchmark** the alternatives
4. Still too slow? Only then rewrite that bottleneck in C++ or Rust

## Profile first: where is the time spent?

Profiling code with [profvis](https://profvis.r-lib.org/).

```r
library(profvis)

profvis({
    counts <- simulateCounts(n_genes = 20000, n_samples = 50)
    cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts, method = "log2cpm")
    res <- testDifferentialExpression(cpm, condition)
})
```

profvis opens an interactive flame graph showing how much **time** and
**memory** each line takes.

. . .

- Usually, a **single function or loop** is responsible for most of the
  run time
- Optimise **that** part only.

## Benchmark: compare alternatives

Once you've found the bottleneck, compare alternative implementations with
[bench](https://bench.r-lib.org/):

```{r}
#| label: bench-r
m <- matrix(rnorm(1e5 * 10), ncol = 10)   # 100,000 genes x 10 samples
colSumsLoop <- function(x) {
    out <- c()
    for (j in seq_len(ncol(x))) {
        s <- 0
        for (i in seq_len(nrow(x))) s <- s + x[i, j]
        out <- c(out, s)
    }
    out
}
bench::mark(
    loop = colSumsLoop(m), apply = apply(m, 2, sum), colSums = colSums(m),
    iterations = 20
)[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc")]
```

## src/: C++ code with Rcpp

For bottlenecks that can't be solved in R, write C++ code with
[Rcpp](https://www.rcpp.org/):

```{r}
#| label: rcpp
Rcpp::cppFunction("
NumericVector colSumsCpp(NumericMatrix x) {
    int nc = x.ncol();
    NumericVector out(nc);
    for (int j = 0; j < nc; j++) {
        out[j] = sum(x(_, j));
    }
    return out;
}")

colSumsCpp(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2))
```

## src/: was it worth it?

Always benchmark your compiled code against the **best R version**:

```{r}
#| label: bench-rcpp
res <- bench::mark(R = colSums(m), Rcpp = colSumsCpp(m), iterations = 50)
res[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc")]
```

## src/: Rcpp inside a package

```r
usethis::use_rcpp()   # creates src/, adds Rcpp to LinkingTo and Imports
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
`src/colsums.cpp`

```cpp
#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector colSumsCpp(NumericMatrix x) {
    ...
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
`R/toyBioc-package.R`

```r
#' @useDynLib toyBioc, .registration = TRUE
#' @importFrom Rcpp sourceCpp
NULL
```

Then `devtools::document()` runs `Rcpp::compileAttributes()`, which
creates `R/RcppExports.R` and `src/RcppExports.cpp`.
:::
::::

## src/: Rust code with rextendr

[rextendr](https://extendr.github.io/rextendr/) does for Rust what Rcpp
does for C++.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```r
## Set up Rust in the package
rextendr::use_extendr()

## After editing src/rust/src/lib.rs
rextendr::document()
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```rust
use extendr_api::prelude::*;

/// @export
#[extendr]
fn hello_rust() -> &'static str {
    "Hello from Rust!"
}

extendr_module! {
    mod toyBioc;
    fn hello_rust;
}
```
:::
::::

Add `SystemRequirements: Cargo (Rust's package manager), rustc` to
  DESCRIPTION

## data/: R objects for examples

```r
## Save an object to data/ (code to create it goes in inst/scripts/)
usethis::use_data(example_counts)
```

Document data sets in `R/data.R`:

```r
#' Example RNA-seq count matrix
#'
#' Simulated counts for 6 genes and 4 samples (2 controls, 2 treated).
#'
#' @format A numeric matrix with 6 rows (genes) and 4 columns (samples).
#' @source Simulated with `inst/scripts/make-counts.R`.
#' @usage data(example_counts)
"example_counts"
```

- **Keep data small**: the package tarball must be **< 10 MB**, and each
  file **≤ 5 MB**
- For larger data, use **ExperimentHub** or an experiment data package


## inst/extdata and inst/scripts

Files in `inst/` are installed as they are. Raw files (e.g., `.tsv`, `.bam`,
`.fasta`) go in `inst/extdata/`. You can find them with `system.file()`:

```{r}
#| label: system-file
#| echo: false
#| include: false
pkgload::load_all(toy_path, quiet = TRUE, export_all = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: extdata
counts_file <- system.file("extdata", "counts.tsv", package = "toyBioc")
counts <- as.matrix(read.delim(counts_file, row.names = 1))
head(counts, 3)
```

. . .

**Document how each file was created** in `inst/scripts/` (data source, URL,
filtering, code), so users can roughly reproduce it.

## Package structure: vignettes/ {.anatomy-slide}

```{r}
#| label: anatomy-vignettes
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat(render_anatomy(c("vignettes")))
```

## vignettes/: long-form documentation

At least one vignette (`.Rmd` or `.qmd`) with **executed** code, using
`BiocStyle::html_document`. Start from `biocthis::use_bioc_vignette()`.
Expected sections:

1. **Introduction**: motivation, what the package does, and how it compares
   with other Bioconductor packages
2. **Installation**: in a chunk that isn't evaluated
   ```r
   if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
       install.packages("BiocManager")
   BiocManager::install("toyBioc")
   ```
3. **Usage (or multiple sections)**: worked examples
4. **Session information**: `sessionInfo()` at the end
5. **References**

## Vignettes: do's and don'ts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
````markdown
## Normalization

```{{r}}
cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts)
```

```{{r, eval=FALSE}}
res <- runAnalysis(big_dataset)
```
````
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
````markdown
## Normalization

Library sizes differ across samples, so raw
counts can't be compared directly. Here, we
normalize them to counts per million (CPM):

```{{r}}
cpm <- normalizeCounts(counts)
colSums(cpm)
```

All columns now sum to 1 million, so
expression levels are comparable across
samples.
````
:::
:::
::::

## Vignettes: a vignette is teaching material

- Put **text before and after every chunk**: what is the code going to do?
  How should the output be interpreted?
- **Execute all chunks**. Static vignettes (`eval = FALSE` everywhere) are
  not accepted
- Use **small example data**. The goal is to show how to use the package,
  not to reproduce a paper's results
- **Don't assume prior knowledge**: explain the data, the classes and the
  biology
- Show a **complete workflow** that users can copy and adapt

## Other files

- `README.md`: shown on GitHub. Say what the package does and how to install
  it
- `NEWS.md`: what changed in each version (shown on the landing page)
- `inst/CITATION`: how to cite your package (e.g., the paper)

# Checking and submitting {background-color="#1a81c2"}

## R CMD check vs BiocCheck

| | `R CMD check` | `BiocCheck` |
|-|---------------|-------------|
| **Check** | R package requirements: installs, examples run, tests pass, docs match code, ... | Bioconductor guidelines: biocViews, version number, vignette, coding practices, formatting, ... |
| **Run with** | `devtools::check()` | `BiocCheck::BiocCheck()` |
| **Examples of issues** | Undocumented arguments, undeclared dependencies, failing tests | `sapply()`, `1:n`, lines > 80 chars, `\dontrun{}`, missing `sessionInfo()` in vignette |

: {.smaller tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

. . .

Your package must pass `R CMD check` and `BiocCheck` with **0 errors and 0
warnings**. Fix NOTEs too, or justify them to the reviewer.

## Running the checks

```r
## In the package directory
devtools::check()                              # R CMD build + R CMD check

## On the package source
BiocCheck::BiocCheck()
```

<br>

Limits to keep in mind:

- `R CMD check` must take **less than 10 minutes**
- Package tarball **< 10 MB**. Individual files **≤ 5 MB**
- Vignettes, examples and tests should use **< 8 GB** of memory
- Develop and test with the **devel** version of Bioconductor

## The submission process

Since 2026, submissions go through
[Bioconductor/BiocContributions](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions),
with builds and checks run by **rOpenSci's R-universe** (GitHub Actions).

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 11
flowchart LR
    A["Open an issue at<br>BiocContributions"] --> B["Automatic<br>precheck"]
    B --> C["Accept policies<br>(/accept-policies)"]
    C --> D["Builds on R-universe<br>(R CMD check,<br>BiocCheck)"]
    D --> E["Review<br>in progress"]
    E --> F["Package<br>accepted"]
    E --> G["Package<br>declined"]
    style F fill:#2e8540,color:#fff
    style G fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
```

Each step is shown as a **label** on your GitHub issue (*precheck-passed*,
*pre-review*, *Build OK* / *Build Error*, *review in progress*, *package
accepted*, ...).

## Submitting, step by step

1. Put your package in a **public GitHub repository** named exactly like the
   package
2. Open an issue at
   [BiocContributions](https://github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions)
   using the **new submission template**, with your repository's URL
3. An **automatic precheck** looks at `DESCRIPTION` (version `x.99.y`,
   `biocViews`, no `Remotes:`), `vignettes/` and file sizes
4. Read the policies posted in the issue and comment **`/accept-policies`**
5. Your repository is copied to the **BiocStaging** organisation and added to
   an R-universe. **From now on, push changes there**
6. **Bump the version** (`0.99.0` → `0.99.1`) with each push to trigger a new
   build. Build reports are posted in the issue

## The review

- A **reviewer** is assigned once there are no build ERRORs (justify any
  remaining WARNINGs or NOTEs in a comment). Label: *review in progress*
- Reviewers are **volunteers** who go through your code, docs and vignette
  against the guidelines
- Reviews usually start **within ~3 weeks** of a clean build, and may take
  several rounds
- If a review stalls and you don't reply, the package may be marked as
  *inactive review* and the issue closed

## The review (cont'd)

Tips:

- **Respond to every comment** in the issue, point by point (what you
  changed, or why you didn't)
- Push all fixes (with a version bump), then comment on the issue
- Think of it as **free code review from experienced developers**.

# Maintaining a package {background-color="#1a81c2"}

## After acceptance

- Your package is moved to **Bioconductor devel**, and you get a
  **BiocCredentials** account to manage the SSH keys for push access
- It goes into the next **release** (April or October)
- Each release creates a **release branch** (bug fixes only) and you keep
  developing on **devel** (new features)
- Version numbers: `x.y.z`, with **even `y`** in release and **odd `y`** in
  devel (e.g., `1.2.0` in release, `1.3.0` in devel). **Bump `z`** with
  every change you push

::: {.mermaid-short}
```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 10
flowchart LR
    A["Submission<br>versions 0.99.z"] -- accepted --> R(("Bioc<br>release"))
    R --> B["devel branch<br>1.1.z: new features"]
    R --> C["RELEASE_3_23 branch<br>1.0.z: bug fixes only"]
    style B fill:#1a81c2,color:#fff
    style C fill:#87b13f,color:#fff
```
:::

## Being a maintainer

- Check the **nightly build reports** and fix errors and warnings quickly
  (failures are sent from `BBS-noreply@bioconductor.org`)
- Answer questions on the [support site](https://support.bioconductor.org/)
  (add your package to your *Watched Tags*)
- Subscribe to the **bioc-devel** mailing list
- Keep the maintainer email in DESCRIPTION up to date
- To remove functions, follow the **deprecation guidelines**
  (`.Deprecated()` → `.Defunct()` across releases)

# Wrapping up {background-color="#1a81c2"}

## Checklist before submitting

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- [ ] In scope, with ≥ 2 biocViews leaf terms
- [ ] Reuses Bioconductor classes
- [ ] Informative `Description` (≥ 3 sentences)
- [ ] Open license
- [ ] Few dependencies, with niche ones in `Suggests`
- [ ] `@importFrom`, not `@import`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- [ ] Every exported function documented, with types and examples
- [ ] Unit tests covering all options and errors
- [ ] Small data, with provenance in `inst/scripts/`
- [ ] Executed vignette that teaches
- [ ] `R CMD check` and `BiocCheck`: 0 errors, 0 warnings
:::
::::
